01.actor: A man's purchaser of a tract of land, facing a creditor
01.event: A creditor repossessed one of two tracts a debtor had sold, then came to repossess the second, so the purchaser went to him with the whole debt in cash.
01.turn: The purchaser offered the creditor a choice: take the tract as full payment or take the money and give up both tracts.
01.outcome: Not shown; the creditor's response is not in the passage.
01.summary: A man owed one hundred dinars and had sold two tracts of land for fifty each. The creditor repossessed one tract, then came for the other. The purchaser took one hundred dinars to the creditor and told him to either value the first tract at the full debt or take the money and give up both.
01.missing: The creditor's answer and how the matter ended.

03.actor: Rabbi Abba bar Shumni and Rav Menashya bar Yirmeya
03.event: Two scholars parting at a river ford agreed each would tell the other a teaching he had not heard, and each opened with one.
03.turn: Their exchange of teachings served as the example of the question asked.
03.outcome: The second scholar's teaching and the exchange are cut off and do not clearly conclude.
03.summary: Two scholars were saying goodbye at the ford of a river. They agreed each would offer a teaching the other had not heard. One defined the drinker as one who can still speak before a king. The other began a teaching about a convert's property, which Rav Sheshet and others then extended.
03.missing: A real turn or ending; it is mostly a series of teachings.

05.actor: A man pining for a woman, in Eretz Yisrael
05.event: A man suffering over a certain woman wanted to leave Eretz Yisrael, but heard the teaching about the great significance of living there.
05.turn: On hearing it, he gave up leaving.
05.outcome: He endured his suffering in the land until the day he died.
05.summary: A man in Eretz Yisrael was tormented by his love for a woman and wanted to leave the land to be with her. When he heard the idea about how significant it is to live in Eretz Yisrael, he stayed and endured his suffering there until his death.

06.event: Rabbi Hanina sent four dinars through his wife to a pauper he supported every Shabbat eve.
06.turn: His wife overheard people in the house asking the man whether he dined on silver or gold tablecloths, and reported he did not need charity.
06.outcome: Rabbi Hanina responded that we should appreciate swindlers, since they spare us from sinning daily by neglecting the truly poor.
06.summary: Rabbi Hanina regularly sent a pauper four dinars. One day his wife took it and came back saying the man did not need it, because she heard people at his house asking whether he dined on silver or gold tablecloths. Rabbi Hanina answered that we should be grateful to swindlers, because without them we would sin every day by not giving to the truly poor.

07.event: Sitting before Rabbi Yannai, Rabbi Hanina Kara said the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda.
07.outcome: Rabbi Yannai told him to go outside and recite his verses there, since the halakha does not follow Rabbi Yehuda.
07.summary: Rabbi Hanina Kara, an expert in Bible, sat before Rabbi Yannai and declared the law follows Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yannai told him to go outside and recite his verses there, because the law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda.

08.event: Rabbi Meir, who used to ridicule transgressors, saw Satan disguised as a woman across a river and crossed a rope bridge toward her.
08.turn: Halfway across, Satan left him and revealed the disguise.
08.outcome: Satan said that only the heavenly proclamation protecting Rabbi Meir and his Torah kept him from destroying him.
08.summary: Rabbi Meir used to mock people who sinned. One day Satan appeared to him as a woman on the far side of a river, and he took a rope bridge to reach her. At the midpoint Satan left him and said that if heaven had not proclaimed to take care of Rabbi Meir and his Torah, his blood would have been made worthless.

09.event: Rav Anan wrote a familiar letter to Rav Huna, who sent back a sharp reply through Rav Sheshet.
09.turn: Rav Anan, offended and not understanding the word marzeiha, consulted Mar Ukva.
09.outcome: Mar Ukva said Anan had taken an improper liberty in addressing Rav Huna and explained that marzeiha means a mourner.
09.summary: Rav Anan sent Rav Huna a letter addressing him as an equal. Rav Huna replied sharply through Rav Sheshet, who relayed it reluctantly. Rav Anan, hurt and puzzled by the word marzeiha, went to Mar Ukva, who told him he had been presumptuous and explained the word means a mourner.

10.event: In Rava's court a woman was obligated to swear, but his wife said she was untrustworthy, and he turned the oath onto the other party. On another occasion Rav Pappa said a document was already paid.
10.turn: Rava would not accept one witness, Rav Pappa, yet had relied on his wife's word because he knew her to be reliable.
10.outcome: Rava explained he knew his wife's honesty with certainty but not Rav Pappa's.
10.summary: A woman had to swear an oath in Rava's court. Rava's wife, the daughter of Rav Hisda, said the woman was known to swear falsely, so Rava shifted the oath to the other side. Later Rav Pappa said a document was already paid, but Rava said one witness is nothing. Rav Adda bar Mattana asked why Rava trusted his wife and not Rav Pappa, and Rava said he knew her honesty for certain, not Pappa's.

11.event: Bonyos sent Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi a measure of a se'a from Na'usa, and the Rabbi measured it.
11.turn: It held 217 eggs, matching none of the standard se'a measures (the context shows this).
11.outcome: The result is left unresolved in the passage.
11.summary: Rav Dimi reported that a man named Bonyos sent Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi a se'a-measure from Na'usa. The Rabbi measured it and found it held 217 eggs, which fits none of the known se'a sizes.
11.missing: What the measurement meant or how it was resolved.

13.actor: A man who made a conditional bill of divorce
13.event: A man told agents that if he did not return within thirty days, the document would be a divorce, and he arrived on the last day.
13.turn: The ferryman was on the far side, so he could not cross in time and shouted to people that he had come.
13.outcome: Shmuel ruled that this was not a return, so the condition was fulfilled.
13.summary: A man set a condition that if he did not return within thirty days, his bill of divorce would take effect. He reached the river bank on the last day but the ferry was on the other side, so he shouted that he had come. Shmuel ruled that this does not count as returning.

14.event: Rabbi Yehuda reported that people drew water on Shabbat from the channel running from Avel to Tzippori by the Elders' authority.
14.turn: The Sages rejected it as proof, since the channel was too small to need a partition.
14.summary: Rabbi Yehuda said that people used to draw water on Shabbat from a channel running from Avel to Tzippori with the Elders' permission and no extra partition. The other Sages replied that this was no proof, because the channel was too small to be a separate domain.
14.missing: Little narrative detail; mainly a cited precedent and its rebuttal.

15.event: A man with a lot of movable property wanted to give it away as a gift and was told he needed to transfer it by means of land.
15.turn: He bought a plot near Jerusalem and designated part of it, with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels, for a named recipient.
15.outcome: He died, and the Sages upheld his statement.
15.summary: A man in Jerusalem wanted to give away a large amount of movable property but was told it could be transferred only along with land. He bought a plot near the city and declared part of it to a certain person together with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels. He then died, and the Sages upheld what he said.

16.actor: Neighbors of a gentile superintendent near Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya
16.event: Neighbors asked a gentile superintendent to rent them his domain and he refused, so they asked whether they could rent it from his wife.
16.turn: Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya and Rav Mattana had no answer.
16.outcome: Rav Yehuda said in Shmuel's name that a man's wife may establish an eiruv without his knowledge.
16.summary: A gentile superintendent who lived near Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya refused to rent his domain to the neighbors. They asked whether they could rent it from his wife, but neither Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya nor Rav Mattana knew. They went to Rav Yehuda, who said Shmuel ruled that a wife may establish an eiruv without her husband's knowledge.

17.event: Ben Azzai found a scroll of lineages in Jerusalem.
17.turn: It recorded that someone was a mamzer, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's teachings, and that Manasseh killed Isaiah.
17.outcome: No further outcome in the passage.
17.summary: Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai said he found a scroll of lineages in Jerusalem. It listed a certain man as a mamzer, praised the teachings of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov as accurate, and recorded that Manasseh killed Isaiah.
17.missing: An actual unfolding story; the passage only reports a discovery and its contents.

18.actor: A man who betrothed a woman
18.event: A man betrothed a woman with a myrtle mat worth less than a peruta.
18.turn: When people objected, he said four dinars wrapped in it would serve; she took it and stayed silent.
18.outcome: Rava ruled her silence after the money was given means nothing, so there was no proven betrothal.
18.summary: A man betrothed a woman using a mat of myrtle branches worth less than a peruta. People objected, so he said she was betrothed with the four dinars in it. She took it and said nothing. Rava ruled that silence after money is given counts for nothing.

20.actor: A purchaser of a mansion facing a creditor
20.event: A creditor repossessed one of two mansions sold for five hundred each, then sought the other, and the purchaser brought the whole thousand to him.
20.turn: The purchaser offered the creditor either to keep the first mansion for the whole debt or take the thousand and release both.
20.outcome: Rami bar Hama and Rava then discussed it, but the creditor's response is not given.
20.summary: A man owed one thousand dinars and sold two mansions for five hundred each. The creditor repossessed one, then went after the other. The purchaser took a thousand dinars to the creditor and told him to either accept the first mansion as full payment or take the money and give up both.
